lesson.title: Seeing the World Only From Where You Stand
lesson.summary: Egocentrism describes the preoperational child's difficulty mentally separating their own viewpoint from other people's, explaining behaviors that look selfish but are actually cognitive limitations.
lesson.body:
You already know that a child in the preoperational stage is still building the mental tools for logical, flexible thought. One striking consequence of that immaturity is egocentrism: the tendency to assume that other people see, know, and feel the same things you do, simply because you haven't yet developed the ability to mentally represent a perspective different from your own. It's important to notice what this term does not mean in psychology. It isn't arrogance or selfishness in the everyday sense; a four-year-old isn't choosing to ignore your feelings out of rudeness. Rather, their mind hasn't yet built the machinery to hold two viewpoints in awareness at once ,  their own and someone else's ,  and compare them.

Think about why this happens. Preoperational thought tends to focus on one salient feature or one viewpoint at a time rather than juggling multiple angles simultaneously. Taking another person's perspective requires exactly that kind of juggling: you have to keep your own view active while also constructing a separate, different mental model of what someone else perceives, and then keep the two distinct. That's a demanding coordination task, and the preoperational child's thinking simply isn't organized to do it yet. So the child defaults to the only viewpoint that's cognitively available ,  their own ,  and projects it outward, assuming it applies to everyone.

Jean Piaget and his colleague Bärbel Inhelder illustrated this with what's often called the three mountains task. A child sits facing a small model of three differently shaped mountains, each with distinct features like snow, a cross, or a house on top. A doll is placed on the opposite side of the model, so it "sees" the mountains from a different angle. When asked to pick out a picture showing what the doll sees, young children in the preoperational range typically choose the picture matching their own view, not the doll's. They aren't being careless; they genuinely have trouble generating a mental image of the scene from a position they aren't physically occupying.

You can see the same pattern in everyday behavior outside the lab. A young child on the phone with a grandparent might hold up a drawing and say "look at this," not registering that the grandparent can't see through the phone. Or during pretend conversation, a child may describe an event using only pronouns like "he" and "it" without naming who "he" is, assuming the listener already has the same picture in mind that the child does. In both cases, the child isn't withholding information deliberately ,  they simply haven't separated their own state of knowledge from the listener's.

As children move beyond the preoperational years, this tendency fades as their thinking becomes more flexible and able to consider multiple perspectives or dimensions at once. That shift ,  being able to mentally step outside your own vantage point and coordinate it with someone else's ,  is one of the key developments that later cognitive stages make possible, and it's worth watching for as you continue through how thinking changes across childhood.
